slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code defines and exports a comprehensive EXIF metadata parser that accesses image binary data and decodes embedded metadata tags including GPS coordinates and camera information. It reads and processes binary image files, decodes base64-encoded image data URIs, and parses XMP metadata if enabled, but does not perform any network, file system, or system execution operations. This behavior facilitates detailed extraction of image metadata for potential privacy analysis or forensic purposes.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a comprehensive EXIF metadata parser that reads and decodes image metadata including GPS, camera info, and XMP data. It operates purely on local image data or data URIs and does not perform any network communication, file system manipulation, or code execution beyond parsing. While it accesses sensitive metadata such as GPS coordinates, it does not exfiltrate or misuse this data. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve network communication, remote code execution, or data exfiltration, this code lacks any such suspicious operations. The presence of detailed EXIF parsing is legitimate and common in image processing libraries. Therefore, there is very low confidence that this code is malicious.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Malicious Weather App (PoC exploiting CVE-2019-2234) (Android APK (Google Play/side-loaded))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, after capturing a photo or video, the code parses EXIF metadata from the media file to extract GPS coordinates, then uploads the location data to a remote C&C server, enabling covert exfiltration of sensitive location information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The app extracts and exfiltrates GPS location data embedded in media files without user consent, enabling tracking of the device's physical location.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal apps do not access or transmit location metadata from photos or videos without explicit user permission and clear disclosure.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Photo management apps may read EXIF data for sorting or mapping, but do not covertly transmit location data to external servers.
key_indicators: Automated EXIF parsing for GPS data in background
Network transmission of extracted location data
No user interaction or notification during data access

package_info.package_versions: All versions prior to patched Google Camera/Samsung Camera apps (pre-July 2019)
package_info.why_malicious: The package exploits a vulnerability in Android camera app intent handling (CVE-2019-2234) to bypass camera and microphone permissions, enabling covert photo, video, and audio capture, as well as exfiltration of sensitive data (including GPS metadata) to a remote C&C server. It maintains persistent C&C communication for remote exploitation, operating without user consent or awareness.

attack_chain.action: Malicious app is installed and establishes a persistent connection to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote attacker can issue commands to the device.

attack_chain.action: Attacker issues command to take a photo, record video, or record audio (including during calls), triggering covert media capture.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device captures sensitive media (photos, videos, audio) without user knowledge.

attack_chain.action: Captured photos and videos are stored in accessible storage; app parses EXIF data for GPS location.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive media and location data are prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: App uploads captured media and extracted GPS/location data to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to private photos, videos, audio, and location data from the device.

behavioral_signatures: Background apps sending camera or video capture intents without holding CAMERA or MICROPHONE permissions
Apps accessing and parsing EXIF GPS metadata from photos or videos without user interaction
Persistent outbound connections to unknown servers from apps not expected to require continuous network access
Media capture events triggered by proximity sensor activity in background services
file_indicators: Unexpected photos or videos appearing in device camera roll or media storage
App accessing camera or media storage without user-initiated action or visible UI
Frequent or automated access to EXIF data in app logs or storage access patterns
network_indicators: Outbound connections to C&C infrastructure (unknown IPs/domains) from non-network-centric apps
Uploads of media files (photos, videos, audio) to remote servers without user action
Persistent TCP connections initiated by background services with no user-facing justification
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for apps that trigger camera or video capture intents without holding CAMERA or MICROPHONE permissions, especially if they only request storage permission. Flag apps that access EXIF GPS metadata or upload media files to external servers without user interaction. Use network monitoring to detect persistent outbound connections from apps not expected to maintain such connections. Alert on media capture events triggered by background services or proximity sensor events, and correlate with lack of user interaction or visible UI.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code initiates an HTTPS GET request to a remote server to download a file named 'initial.png', accumulates the response data, decodes the base64-encoded content, and executes it using eval, resulting in remote code execution and enabling the delivery of a second-stage payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code automatically fetches and executes remote content at import-time, using eval on data received from an untrusted external domain. This is a classic remote code execution pattern and is highly indicative of malware staging.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate CORS parser should not perform any network requests or execute remote code during import. Such behavior is entirely outside the expected functionality of a CORS utility.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic plugin systems may fetch and execute code, but only from trusted, verifiable sources and with explicit user consent, never at import-time without user interaction.
key_indicators: Import-time network request to untrusted external domain
Base64 decoding and dynamic execution of remote content using eval
No user interaction or consent required for code execution
Obfuscated or minified code structure in index.js

package_info.why_malicious: The package is explicitly designed to act as a dropper for multi-stage malware. Upon import, it downloads and executes remote code disguised as PNG images, which are actually platform-specific backdoors. It uses steganography and code execution techniques to implant persistent malware on both Windows and Unix systems, violating user trust, enabling remote access, and compromising system security.

attack_chain.action: Initial package import triggers a network request to download and execute remote code from 'initial.png' using eval.
attack_chain.leads_to: Stage 2 payload execution

attack_chain.action: Stage 2 payload downloads and executes platform-specific backdoor binaries disguised as PNG files, targeting Windows and Unix systems.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and remote access established

attack_chain.action: Persistence mechanisms are established via registry autorun modification on Windows or shell profile (.zshrc) modification on Unix.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor remains active across system reboots

behavioral_signatures: Import-time network requests to untrusted domains
Base64 decoding and eval execution of remote content
Downloading and executing files with image extensions as binaries
Persistence via registry autorun or shell profile modification
Writing executables to uncommon locations such as /var/tmp or C:/ProgramData with misleading file extensions
file_indicators: index.js containing minified or obfuscated network/eval logic
Downloaded files named *.png but containing binary or script content
/var/tmp/logd (Unix backdoor binary)
C:/ProgramData/thumbs.db (Windows DLL backdoor)
Modifications to .zshrc (Unix) or registry autorun keys (Windows)
network_indicators: api.jz-aws.info (all subdomains and paths)
HTTPS requests for .png files from api.jz-aws.info or similar non-image hosting domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that initiate network requests at import or install time, especially to suspicious domains like api.jz-aws.info. Flag code that decodes and executes remote content using eval. Detect files with image extensions being written and executed as binaries, particularly in uncommon locations such as /var/tmp or C:/ProgramData. Watch for unauthorized modifications to autorun registry keys or shell profile files (.zshrc, .bashrc). Network monitoring should alert on requests to api.jz-aws.info or similar suspicious infrastructure, especially for .png files that are not valid images.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code initiates an HTTPS GET request to a remote server to download a file named 'initial.png', decodes the base64 content, and executes it using eval, resulting in immediate remote code execution and enabling the delivery of a stage 2 payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs a network request to a hardcoded external domain at import-time, decodes the response as base64, and executes it dynamically with eval. This pattern is a textbook example of remote code execution and malware staging, as it allows the attacker to deliver and run arbitrary code on the victim's system without user interaction.

It abuses import-time execution to fetch and run remote code disguised as PNG images, which are actually malicious payloads. The code uses steganography and dynamic code execution to implant persistent malware on both Windows and Unix systems, violating user trust and security boundaries by enabling remote code execution, persistence, and system compromise.

slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code defines a client-side image compression utility that accesses file input elements in the DOM, reads image files using FileReader, draws images onto a canvas for resizing and compression, and converts compressed images back to base64 and Blob formats. It accesses image metadata via the previously defined EXIF parser but does not perform any network communication or system execution. This behavior enables client-side image processing and metadata extraction without external data transmission.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a client-side image compression utility that reads image files from a file input element, processes them using canvas to resize and compress, and converts images to base64 and Blob formats. It does not perform any network communication, system manipulation, or code execution beyond standard browser APIs. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks key indicators such as obfuscated payloads, eval-based code execution, remote network requests, or unauthorized data exfiltration. The use of FileReader, canvas, and base64 encoding is typical for image processing utilities and not inherently suspicious. Although the code is minified and somewhat obfuscated, this is common in client-side libraries and does not imply malicious intent here. Therefore, there is very low confidence that this code is malicious.

attack_chain.action: Extracted C2 payload registers the client with the attacker's server, polls for commands, executes them, and exfiltrates results.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of the infected system and exfiltration of command output.

behavioral_signatures: Postinstall script spawns detached Node.js processes using spawn/unref
Image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg) are read and parsed for ASCII payloads during installation
Dynamic code execution via new Function() on data extracted from image files
Outbound HTTPS connections to hardcoded IP address 85.208.108.29 for registration, polling, and result exfiltration
Periodic polling for remote commands and execution of arbitrary shell commands
file_indicators: dist/loadformat.js
index.js containing spawn/unref logic targeting dist/loadformat.js
logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg in package root directory
References to analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte variables in code
network_indicators: Outbound POST requests to /register and /post-result endpoints
Outbound GET requests to /get-command?clientId=
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that, during installation, spawn detached Node.js processes, read and parse image files for ASCII payloads, or dynamically execute code extracted from non-code files. Flag packages making outbound connections to hardcoded or suspicious IPs (e.g., 85.208.108.29) or exhibiting periodic polling for remote commands. Scan package contents for the presence of suspicious image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg) and loader scripts (dist/loadformat.js), and inspect for code patterns involving analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte.
